one_liner: Small C++11 UTF-8 JSON DOM library with an re2c scanner; parses about 2x and prints 3.5-4.5x faster than nlohmann/json 2.0.3.
what_it_does: Parses UTF-8 JSON into an immutable ujson::value (null, bool, double, string, array, object) and writes it back compact or indented, ASCII-escaped or UTF-8. Arrays are std::vector<value>, objects are std::vector<std::pair<std::string, value>> sorted by key, and data is pulled out with free casts (bool_cast, double_cast, int32_cast, string_cast, array_cast, object_cast) that throw on a type mismatch. Not a drop-in for nlohmann/json: there is no operator[], no mutable tree and no serializer-from-struct machinery beyond a to_json hook for vectors and maps.
how_it_is_fast: The tokenizer is a re2c-generated DFA that validates UTF-8 (including \u escapes and surrogate pairs) while it scans, so strings are copied without a second validation pass; with SSE2 it skips whitespace and copies escape-free string runs 16 bytes at a time (_mm_cmpeq_epi8 + movemask). Numbers go through Google's double-conversion (StringToDouble / ToShortest) instead of strtod/printf. Values use a small-object buffer (null, bool, double and, on libc++/MSVC, strings up to 22/15 bytes stay inline) and arrays, objects and long strings sit behind std::shared_ptr, so copies only bump a reference count; the writer appends into one std::string.
when_to_use: Legacy C++11 code that wants a small, readable, MIT-licensed DOM parser and writer with strict UTF-8 validation, built with clang/libc++ or MSVC.
Serialization-heavy jobs on moderate documents where stringify/prettify speed matters more than lookup speed (24.9 ms stringify vs 87.7 ms for nlohmann 2.0.3 on the three shootout files).
Configuration or message data you treat as immutable values and pass by value between threads (shared_ptr payloads, no mutation).
Read-once documents whose objects are small enough that sorted-vector binary search is fine.
when_not_to_use: Anything built with GCC/libstdc++ 5 or newer without first testing it: the header assumes libstdc++ strings are copy-on-write and relocates them with memcpy (see gotchas).
Untrusted input: the parser is unbounded recursive descent (deep nesting can overflow the stack), and the library has had no fixes since 2016-10-08.

Data with 64-bit integers or exact integer round-trips: every number is a double, so 1234567890123456789 comes back as 1.2345678901234568e18 and -0.0/0.0 print as -0/0 (nativejson-benchmark roundtrip 18/27).
Large numeric arrays or memory-constrained parsing: the measured build used 34.4 MB for canada.json against nlohmann's 5.3 MB, and RapidJSON, yyjson or simdjson parse several times faster.
Code that traverses or queries the DOM a lot: tree statistics were 1.4x slower than nlohmann (3.02 vs 2.17 ms) because every type test is a virtual call and string access uses dynamic_cast.

integration.dependencies: bundled double-conversion 1.1.5 (BSD-3-Clause amalgamation); re2c only if you edit ujson.re2c; Catch for the tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 with RTTI (string_cast uses dynamic_cast); README tables list clang 3.4 (Xcode 5.1.1), gcc 4.8.3 and VS2013; the CMake script needs CMake 2.8 policies and downloads re2c 0.13.5 from SourceForge
integration.platforms: any for the scalar path; SSE2 fast paths on x86/x86-64 (GCC/Clang __SSE2__, MSVC x64 or /arch:SSE2); only libc++, MSVC STL and libstdc++ are recognised (other standard libraries hit #error)
integration.thread_safety: README: values are immutable and arrays/objects/long strings are shared through std::shared_ptr, so passing a ujson::value by value to another thread is race-free; no other guarantees documented

gotchas: find(object, name) and at(object, name) are a bare std::lower_bound with no equality check: for a missing key, find returns the next larger key instead of end(), and at only throws when the key would sort after every member, despite the README saying at 'behaves like std::map::at'. Compare it->first yourself.

By code reading (not executed): with libstdc++ (__GLIBCXX__) the header picks its 'ref-counted string' path and stores a std::string inline, but moves, swaps and the stable_sort of object members relocate values with memcpy. GCC 5+ libstdc++ defaults to the SSO std::string, whose data pointer points into the object itself, so a moved short string keeps pointing at the old storage and its destructor can free a non-heap pointer. The independent benchmark only built it with clang/libc++ on macOS, where strings use ujson's own inline buffer.

The measured snapshot (0d6259e, 2015-04-12) reserved 16 slots in every parsed array and object, which explains the 34.4 MB canada.json footprint (about 56k two-number arrays at 16 x 32-byte values, inferred from code and page data); the author removed the reserve in 65df934 on 2016-10-08 ('slight reduction in parse speed') and the benchmark's sample was never rerun. Escaped '/' was also unsupported in that snapshot (pass01 failure, fixed in 3d1852b).
Objects are stable-sorted on construction, so output key order differs from input, duplicate keys are kept side by side, and every parsed object pays a sort plus a temporary buffer.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against taoJSON (41.2 ms parse) and udp/json-parser (47.3 ms) on the same shootout it parses a little faster (37.2 ms) and stringifies faster than both, but RapidJSON, json.h, yyjson and simdjson are far faster and still maintained; pick ujson only for its small immutable-value API and strict UTF-8 validation, and prefer taoJSON or Boost.JSON for new code.
verified_claims_summary: In Milo Yip's nativejson-benchmark sample of 2016-09-09 (clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS, premake optimize Full with NDEBUG and -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ), ujson snapshot 0d6259e parsed canada, citm_catalog and twitter in 37.15 ms total against 72.48 ms for nlohmann/json 2.0.3 (1.95x), stringified in 24.86 vs 87.73 ms (3.5x) and prettified in 29.28 vs 130.56 ms (4.5x), while DOM traversal was 1.4x slower and parse memory up to 6.5x higher. The current code (65df934) has not been measured.
status_note: Abandoned since 2016-10-08 (12 commits, issue tracker no longer served by Bitbucket); MIT and only four source files, but treat the libstdc++ string path and the find/at lookup as bugs to fix before vendoring.
